rows.practice: chooses suitable qualitative or quantitative methods for a research question, summarises crime and victimisation data and uses it to weigh competing criminological theories
rows.knowledge: the core criminological theories, how victimisation and criminalisation come about and how police, courts, prisons and probation agencies operate and change
rows.identity: a criminology student who reflects on the moral and ethical risks of own research and uses human rights to judge efforts to keep people safe

rows.practice: critiques the explanatory philosophy of published crime studies and applies criminological concepts to design own research, choosing methods accurately for each problem
rows.knowledge: a critical grasp of how inequality, governance, risk and rights shape responses to lawbreakers and of the political weight carried by competing readings of crime data
rows.identity: a critical criminologist who sees the ethical stakes of every method and holds justice agencies to human rights standards with exceptional rigour

rows.practice: selects methodologies for complex crime problems and designs and completes an original empirical study, systematic review or case study in a real-world justice setting
rows.knowledge: a systematic understanding of criminological topics, the history and cultural setting of its ideas and how overlapping forms of power shape the work of justice agencies
rows.identity: an independent researcher of crime and justice who carries critical debate forward with some originality and stays alert to power in own work (ing's reading)

digest.definition: Criminology studies how people and acts are criminalised and victimised, what crime, harm and deviance mean and what causes them, how they are prevented and managed and how they are represented
distinctiveFeatures: Criminology studies how people and acts are criminalised and victimised, what crime, harm and deviance mean and what causes them, how they are prevented and managed and how they are represented
A multidisciplinary field first taught in the UK at postgraduate level from the late 1950s; undergraduate degrees came later
Its theories and areas of enquiry keep changing, fed by staff research and by neighbouring subjects such as sociology, law and philosophy, while its core stays steady
Theoretical and empirical at once, with practical application; many of its theoretical advances have come from empirical studies
Marked by debate over how to explain its subject, put theory into research, inform policy and human rights, handle data and manage research ethics
Contested values in what counts as crime, harm, criminalisation and victimisation lie at its centre
Joins scholarship and practice, working with justice agencies, government and charities in research and teaching partnerships
Its material is often emotive and distressing, so ethics and care run through its teaching and research
Taught as single or joint honours, with foundation degrees leading towards the honours standard and master's degrees going beyond it

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: Inclusion is part of the subject matter (discrimination, colonialism, bias in justice) and a duty on course teams: embedded curricula, belonging, safe dialogue on sensitive topics, review for barriers and attention to a diverse intake (D1, 1.9 to 1.14)

Sustainability means both a current curriculum (green, queer and southern criminology, zemiology) and education for sustainable development: green criminology, ethics, global citizenship and placements linked to sustainability (D1, 1.15 to 1.23)
Named with employability: methodological and research-ethics skills, wide career routes including policing and probation and employability opportunities with safeguards (D1, 1.24 to 1.27)
Varied entry routes and a single-tier approach: adjustments, varied formats for all, fair access to fieldwork and placements, accessible materials and criteria (D1, 2.17; 2.18; 3.5)

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: embedding equality, diversity and inclusion in the curriculum
statements.paraphrase: Criminology staff carry a responsibility to make inclusion real in practice as well as in theory; the study of equality, diversity and inclusion must run through and across curricula, and the discipline must work to make learning, design and delivery inclusive.

forPractitioner.text: Embed the study of equality, diversity and inclusion in every part of the curriculum, not one module, and make design and delivery inclusive; staff share a duty to practise inclusion, and equality law applies to students and staff alike.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: inclusive learning design
statements.paraphrase: Equality and diversity must be built in when courses and curricula are planned and designed, for instance through equity in design and evaluation, safe spaces for students to voice views, student input to assessment and delivery and a curriculum that is flexible and accessible; students will be treated with respect as individual learners and may share in creating knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: Build equality and diversity into the planning and design stage through learning design: equity in course evaluation, safe settings for discussion, student input to assessment and delivery and a curriculum that is flexible, accessible and offered in several modes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: belonging and safe dialogue across the learning journey
statements.paraphrase: Equality and diversity should be revisited at every stage of study, and the discipline must make sure students feel they belong and that their experience adds to their learning; students should be helped to voice views on sensitive and contested topics in a safe, collegial setting and to reflect on how their experience shapes them, and criminology should look critically at widening links with outside communities.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for belonging at each stage: students must feel their experience is an asset, not a barrier. Support open discussion of sensitive and controversial topics safely, help students see how their experience shapes their views and widen engagement with outside communities at undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: inclusive review and removing barriers
statements.paraphrase: Equality and diversity should underpin how the discipline is practised and delivered; inclusion must be treated as continuing quality review and enhancement, course teams must look for hidden or open barriers to success for some groups and for changes that would welcome under-represented groups; teams should build an environment with role models, active support and careful language.

forPractitioner.text: Treat inclusion as part of every review: course teams must check for hidden or overt barriers that hold back particular groups and plan changes to welcome under-represented students, and should provide visible staff role models, active support and considered language.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: attention to under-represented groups
statements.paraphrase: Criminology draws students from many backgrounds, including mature students, those from non-traditional or less affluent backgrounds, carers and disabled students; more attention should go to under-represented groups at every stage from recruitment to after graduation, so that inclusive practice is seen inside and outside the institution.

forPractitioner.text: Pay deliberate attention to under-represented groups across recruitment, marketing, teaching and career support through to after graduation, so that inclusive practice is visible to students and to the outside world.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: keeping the curriculum current
statements.paraphrase: For the discipline to last, its purpose needs to be clear; a course's internal sustainability should rest not only on recruitment but on a current curriculum that takes in new theoretical and methodological work such as green, queer and southern criminology, indigenous knowledge and zemiology.

forPractitioner.text: Judge a course's sustainability by more than recruitment: keep the curriculum current, bringing in emerging approaches such as green, queer and southern criminology, indigenous knowledge and zemiology.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: green criminology in the curriculum
statements.paraphrase: Green criminology, which studies crime that harms the environment, ecological justice and environmental law, has grown in influence; curriculum design should consider its perspectives.

forPractitioner.text: Consider green criminology when designing the curriculum: crimes against the environment, ecological justice and environmental law, including individual, corporate and state failings.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: proactive, partnership-based sustainable education
statements.paraphrase: Criminology joins scholarship and practice, and sustainable education means working with justice agencies, practitioners and other sectors and cultures; together with justice agencies at home and abroad, the discipline should aim to act ahead of problems rather than only react, and should consider innovation and shared concepts and practice, pedagogy included.

forPractitioner.text: Link theory to practice through work with criminal justice agencies, practitioners and other sectors; aim for a curriculum that anticipates problems rather than reacting, and consider innovation in concepts, practice and pedagogy when developing courses.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: ethics in course development
statements.paraphrase: Ethics runs through teaching, research and the discipline's theory and methods, and is tied to sustainability; it should be considered when courses are developed, updated and reviewed, not least because emotive topics call for a careful balance of equality, diversity, open-mindedness, impartiality and accessibility.

forPractitioner.text: Consider ethics at each stage of developing, updating and reviewing a course, and plan how emotive topics will be taught with care for equality, openness, impartiality and accessibility.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: multidisciplinarity guiding curriculum and teaching
statements.paraphrase: Understanding that criminology draws on many disciplines should guide curriculum development and teaching methods, helping learners grasp critically how culture, economy, environment and globalisation connect.

forPractitioner.text: Let criminology's multidisciplinary nature guide curriculum and teaching methods, so that students learn to see critically how culture, the economy, the environment and globalisation interlock.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: knowledge for sustainable development and global citizenship
statements.paraphrase: Criminology should also give students knowledge across topics such as poverty, social justice and environmental and social harm, building awareness of sustainable development and global citizenship and the skills to act on social, environmental and economic concerns.

forPractitioner.text: Offer content on poverty, social justice and environmental and social harms, so that students gain awareness of sustainable development and global citizenship and the skills to address such concerns.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: volunteering and placements for sustainability
statements.paraphrase: Criminology students build skills such as critical thinking, argument and listening that matter for global citizenship and for justice and security work; where possible they should be encouraged to take up volunteering or placements linked to sustainability, and such learning can sit inside modules.

forPractitioner.text: Where possible, encourage volunteering and work placements connected with sustainability, and consider building service and work-based learning into modules.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: methodological skills at honours level
statements.paraphrase: Honours students in criminology are expected to build skills for grasping methodological concepts and principles, including how theory relates to method in research and specialist knowledge of what criminal justice agencies do.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for honours students to develop methodological understanding, including the link between theory and methods and specialist knowledge of the roles and practices of criminal justice agencies.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to build the skills to understand research methods and their principles, including how theory and methods connect, and to learn in some depth what criminal justice agencies do and how.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Criminology degree

statements.about: employability opportunities
statements.paraphrase: Chances for students to build employability skills should be offered at a suitable point, through placements, volunteering, employability-linked assessment or guest speakers; safeguards protect students from exploitation or harassment at work, and it matters that placement employers consider accessibility and reasonable adjustments.

forPractitioner.text: Offer employability opportunities at a fitting point in the course, inside or outside the formal curriculum, with safeguards against exploitation and harassment and attention to accessibility and reasonable adjustments on placements.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: methodological concepts and principles
statements.paraphrase: Because research and critical enquiry underpin criminology, students are expected to build skills for grasping methodological concepts and principles, including how theory, evidence and method relate.

forPractitioner.text: Design the research methods strand so that students build an understanding of methodological concepts and of the relationship between theory, evidence and methods.

forBeneficiary.text: Research and critical enquiry are at the heart of criminology, so you are expected to build the skills to understand research methods, including how theory, evidence and methods fit together.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.appliesTo: honours students at the threshold level
statements.about: philosophy of explanation and research strategies (threshold)
statements.paraphrase: At the threshold level (set jointly with typical) students are expected to understand arguments about explanation in criminological research; ontology and epistemology; the split between qualitative and quantitative research, with mixed methods; inductive and deductive reasoning; they should also be able to tell which data collection and analysis methods suit which research questions.

forPractitioner.text: By threshold, students should grasp the philosophy of explanation; ontology and epistemology; the qualitative-quantitative distinction, with mixed methods; inductive and deductive reasoning. They should also be able to match methods of data collection and analysis to research questions.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should understand the debates about how criminological research explains things, the difference between qualitative and quantitative research, including ways of mixing them; you should also be able to pick methods that suit a research question.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.appliesTo: honours students at the typical level
statements.about: philosophy of explanation and research strategies (typical)
statements.paraphrase: The issuer sets the same research-philosophy expectation for the typical level as for threshold: understanding debates on explanation, ontology and epistemology, research strategies, mixed methods and induction and deduction; and being able to match methods to questions.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, expect the same grasp of research philosophy and strategy as at threshold, shown more securely; most students should be able to justify their choice of methods for a question.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the typical standard, you should understand the debates about explanation in criminological research and the main research strategies; you should also be able to explain clearly why a method suits your question.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.appliesTo: honours students at the excellent level
statements.about: critique of research philosophy (excellent)
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent (first-class) level students are expected not only to discuss how theory and method relate but to critique and apply criminological concepts in designing research; they should be able to criticise the explanatory philosophy of criminological studies and see the ethical stakes of methods and the political weight of different readings of data.

forPractitioner.text: At first-class level, students should go beyond discussing theory and method: they critique and apply criminological concepts in research design, critique the philosophy of explanation in studies and weigh the ethics of methods and the politics of interpreting findings.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the excellent standard, you should be able to critique how criminological studies explain things, use criminological ideas to design research and see the ethical side of your methods and the political side of how findings are read.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: research competence at postgraduate level
statements.paraphrase: At postgraduate level students are expected to grasp key methodological concepts, critique and apply criminological thought in research design and recognise subtle debates, with a wider range of skills than undergraduates and the ability to design and carry out research in real-world settings using many methods.

forPractitioner.text: At postgraduate level, expect students to critique and apply concepts in research design, engage with nuanced methodological debates and design and run criminological research in real settings with a wide repertoire of methods.

forBeneficiary.text: At postgraduate level, you are expected to critique and apply criminological ideas when designing research, follow subtle debates about method and design and carry out real-world research using a wide range of methods.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: foundations of research design and reflexivity
statements.paraphrase: Early in the degree students are expected to have grounding, for both qualitative and quantitative methods, in forming research questions, designing research and reflecting on design and practice, with attention to positionality and power.

forPractitioner.text: In early methods teaching, cover forming a research question, designing a study and reflecting on design and practice, with explicit attention to positionality and power, across qualitative and quantitative traditions.

forBeneficiary.text: Early on, you are expected to learn how to form a research question, design a study and reflect on your research, thinking about your own position and the power differences involved.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: basic knowledge of qualitative approaches
statements.paraphrase: At a basic level students are expected to know the range of qualitative approaches available; the issuer's list is illustrative, running from case studies, interviews, focus groups, observation and ethnography to participatory, decolonising, internet, visual and evaluation methods, sampling, indexing and interpreting qualitative data.

forPractitioner.text: Introduce the main qualitative approaches early, choosing from a broad menu that includes interviewing, focus groups, observation, ethnography (virtual too), participatory and decolonising methods, documentary, visual and internet research, sampling and the limits of interpretation.

forBeneficiary.text: Early on, you are expected to know the main qualitative approaches, such as interviews, focus groups, observation and ethnography, and how qualitative data are sampled, organised and interpreted.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: advanced qualitative analysis
statements.paraphrase: In the later, more advanced stages, students would be expected to show knowledge, and perhaps use, of some qualitative techniques and software, such as coding, analysis and interpretation, using packages like ATLAS.ti or NVivo.

forPractitioner.text: In later years, give students the chance to know and possibly use techniques for coding, analysing and interpreting qualitative data, with software such as ATLAS.ti or NVivo.

forBeneficiary.text: Later in your studies, you would be expected to know, and perhaps use, some techniques for coding, analysing and interpreting qualitative data, possibly with software such as NVivo.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: basic knowledge of quantitative techniques
statements.paraphrase: For quantitative methods, early in the degree students are expected to know some of the techniques available, illustratively questionnaire design, survey sampling, experimental design, evaluation, statistical software, comparing means, correlation and causation, secondary data and descriptive and inferential statistics.

forPractitioner.text: Introduce basic quantitative techniques early, drawing on a menu such as questionnaire design, survey sampling, experimental design and trials, statistical software (for example SPSS or R), comparing means, correlation versus causation, secondary data and basic statistical tests.

forBeneficiary.text: Early on, you are expected to know some basic quantitative techniques, such as designing a questionnaire, sampling, using statistics software, telling correlation from causation and running simple statistical tests.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: advanced quantitative techniques
statements.paraphrase: In the later, more advanced stages, students would be expected to show knowledge, and perhaps use, of some quantitative techniques such as t-tests, ANOVA and other multivariate analysis, systematic reviews, secondary and big data, data mapping, graphical presentation and online data analysis.

forPractitioner.text: In later years, offer some advanced quantitative techniques, such as t-tests, ANOVA, multivariate analysis, systematic reviewing, big and secondary data, mapping, data visualisation and analysis of social media data.

forBeneficiary.text: Later in your studies, you would be expected to know, and perhaps use, some advanced quantitative techniques, such as t-tests, ANOVA, systematic reviews, mapping data or analysing online data.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: methods in practice at higher or postgraduate level
statements.paraphrase: At higher or postgraduate level there is a further expectation of knowing and understanding, and perhaps using in practice, computer-assisted personal interviewing, qualitative software, systematic reviews and virtual ethnography.

forPractitioner.text: At higher or postgraduate level, give students knowledge and understanding, and where possible practice, of computer-assisted interviewing, qualitative analysis software, systematic reviewing and virtual ethnography.

forBeneficiary.text: At a higher or postgraduate stage, you are expected to know and understand, and may use, methods such as computer-assisted interviewing, qualitative analysis software, systematic reviews and online ethnography.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: mixing data and the stages of analysis
statements.paraphrase: All students should also acquire a basic grasp of two things: how qualitative and quantitative data can be combined, including triangulation, data integration and inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning; and the stages of analysis from reduction and display to comparison and integration.

forPractitioner.text: Teach every student the basics of mixing qualitative and quantitative data (triangulation and integration), of induction, deduction and abduction and of the stages of data analysis.

forBeneficiary.text: You should gain a basic understanding of how numerical and qualitative data can be combined, of reasoning by induction, deduction and abduction and of the stages of analysing data.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: knowledge of research ethics and codes
statements.paraphrase: Ethics is basic to all research; at every level students are expected to know what ethics means, the policy frameworks, the difference between personal, legal and professional ethics and the main codes criminologists use, and should show they can discuss the value and limits of codes; they are also expected to know how to get ethical approval locally.

forPractitioner.text: Teach ethics at every level: what ethics means, policy frameworks, the split between individual, legal and professional ethics and the main codes (such as the British Society of Criminology's); students should show they can discuss what codes achieve and where they fall short, and know your institution's approval process.

forBeneficiary.text: At every stage, you are expected to know what research ethics means and the main codes criminologists use; you should be able to discuss what those codes do well and badly, and know how to get ethical approval for your own research.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: strategies for ethical problems
statements.paraphrase: Ethical problems include interviews that revive painful experiences, using material without consent and steering data towards a favoured theory; students are expected to be able to weigh up approaches such as a fitting research design, informed or valid consent, confidentiality and ethical approaches to hard-to-reach and vulnerable groups.

forPractitioner.text: Use common ethical problems, such as distress in interviews, lack of consent and biased handling of data, to teach strategies: suitable design, informed consent, confidentiality and protocols for hard-to-reach and vulnerable groups.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to be able to think through ways of handling ethical problems in research, such as choosing a suitable design, getting informed consent, keeping things confidential and working carefully with vulnerable people.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: the limits of ethical strategies
statements.paraphrase: At higher and postgraduate levels students are expected to see that these strategies are not simple, for instance when confidentiality cannot be guaranteed or has to be broken; there should also be awareness of ways to minimise harm and protect confidentiality.

forPractitioner.text: At higher and postgraduate levels, push students to see the limits of ethical strategies, such as when confidentiality has to be broken, and to know ways of minimising harm and safeguarding confidentiality.

forBeneficiary.text: At a higher or postgraduate stage, you are expected to see that ethical strategies are rarely simple, for example when confidentiality cannot be kept, and you should know ways to reduce harm and protect confidentiality.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: ethics debates and data protection law
statements.paraphrase: At higher and postgraduate levels students are expected to know the wider debates on ethics, such as whether discipline codes are needed, and to know what the law and personal ethics require, including current data protection law and its research exemptions.

forPractitioner.text: At higher and postgraduate levels, cover debates about codes of ethics and what data protection law requires of researchers, including relevant principles and exemptions.

forBeneficiary.text: At a higher or postgraduate stage, you are expected to know the debates about research ethics codes and what data protection law asks of you as a researcher.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: ethical literacy
statements.paraphrase: Overall, all students are expected to reach a suitable level of ethical literacy so that research participants stay safe and well.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure every student reaches a level of ethical literacy fit for keeping research participants safe and well.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to become ethically literate enough to keep the people in your research safe and well.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: accessible, single-tier teaching and assessment
statements.paraphrase: Teaching methods depend on course aims; a two-tier system singling out students with extra needs must be avoided, so teaching and assessment may be tailored, varied formats should be offered to all and expectations should be clear; reasonable adjustments should be considered for fieldwork, equal access to trips, placements and volunteering pursued and assessment criteria should be clear and accessible.

forPractitioner.text: Avoid a two-tier system: offer varied formats to all students, keep expectations transparent, tailor teaching and assessment where needed, consider reasonable adjustments for fieldwork, reduce hidden costs of trips and placements and give clear, accessible assessment criteria at each stage.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: progression from foundations to graduate skills
statements.paraphrase: Early in the degree students are expected to build core theoretical knowledge and basic study skills, then strengthen analysis, interpretation and communication and by graduation show problem-solving, evaluation and reflection and the attributes for self-managed, lifelong learning.

forPractitioner.text: Sequence the course so that core theory and study skills come first, analysis, interpretation and communication grow next and problem-solving, evaluation, reflection and self-managed learning are shown by graduation.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to start with core theory and study skills, build your analysis, interpretation and communication as you go and by the end show that you can solve problems, evaluate, reflect and manage your own learning.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: progress towards the threshold and readiness for postgraduate study
statements.paraphrase: Across an honours degree, which the issuer places at FHEQ level 6 and FQHEIS level 10, students move through the years under each institution's rules, each year expected to build towards the threshold subject-specific and generic skills; a graduate with a second-class degree or better would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study in criminology or a related field.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each year to move students towards the threshold subject-specific and generic skills; those finishing with a second-class degree or higher would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study.

forBeneficiary.text: Each year of your degree is meant to build towards the minimum skills for the award, and if you finish with a second-class degree or better you would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: joint honours outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Joint honours students will attain the core subject-specific and generic skills of criminology, add others from their second subject and may explore where the two meet.

forPractitioner.text: In joint honours courses, students will reach the core specific and generic criminology skills; plan for the skills the other subject adds and for interdisciplinary work where the two overlap.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study criminology with another subject, you will gain the core criminology skills, add skills from your other subject and may explore where the two overlap.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: specialising and independent work later in the course
statements.paraphrase: As students progress, chances to specialise are expected to grow; higher levels should help them deepen analytical and critical skills, core and optional modules will let them build expertise and assessed independent study such as a dissertation will normally come near the end.

forPractitioner.text: Increase specialisation as students progress: higher levels should deepen analysis and critique, core and optional modules will let students focus and an assessed independent project, empirical, policy-based or theoretical, normally comes near the end.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: independent research and reflection on its risks
statements.paraphrase: Most criminology degrees ask students to do some independent research, usually a project or dissertation late in the course, which calls for mature, intelligent reflection on its risks and its moral and ethical issues.

forPractitioner.text: Where the course includes a project or dissertation, prepare students to reflect critically on its risks and its moral and ethical issues before they start.

forBeneficiary.text: Most courses ask you to carry out independent research, such as a dissertation, near the end; you need to reflect maturely and critically on its risks and its ethical issues.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Criminology degree

statements.about: external review
statements.paraphrase: Externality is key to UK quality assurance; providers will use external reviewers in periodic review to gain an outside view of proposed changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Include external reviewers in periodic review so that proposed changes get an outside view and threshold standards and subject content are checked.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: accessible learning materials
statements.paraphrase: Students meet course materials in many ways and modes, full or part-time, with core texts, journals and online resources; it matters that these materials are accessible.

forPractitioner.text: Check that every learning resource, printed, online or streamed, is accessible to all students in every mode of study.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: theory as a core of the degree
statements.paraphrase: Criminology is neither purely deductive nor descriptive: theory guides data collection and interpretation and has to rest on evidence, so students get chances to think abstractly and concretely and link the two; theory is expected to be a core, foundational part of any criminology degree.

forPractitioner.text: Make criminological theory a foundational, core strand of the degree, and give students repeated practice moving between abstract theory and concrete evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: weighing rival interpretations of evidence
statements.paraphrase: Evidence in criminology often fits rival theories, so students are required to weigh alternative readings by how well they match the evidence, their logic, how they sit with other findings and how much they explain, and are given chances to test and revise their own ideas.

forPractitioner.text: Students must weigh competing interpretations against evidence, logic, fit with other findings and explanatory power; give them repeated chances to rehearse and revise their own positions.

forBeneficiary.text: You are required to weigh rival explanations of the same evidence, judging them by how well they fit the evidence and other findings, how logical they are and how much they explain, and to test and revise your own ideas.

statements.about: engaging with public disputes and with values
statements.paraphrase: Criminology mirrors current social, political and public disputes, so students get chances to reflect on their own values and those around them and on how values shape rival readings of evidence; learning, teaching and assessment should let students engage with these disputes and apply criminological knowledge to current crime problems.

forPractitioner.text: Design learning, teaching and assessment so that students engage with live social and political disputes, reflect on their own values and apply criminological knowledge to current crime problems.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: inclusive strategies and distressing content
statements.paraphrase: Students come from diverse backgrounds with varying needs, so courses need flexible, varied strategies giving all as equal a chance as possible; approaches should be designed to be inclusive enough to make alternative assessment unnecessary, and everyone teaching should recognise the emotive nature of the subject and the impact of distressing content.

forPractitioner.text: Use flexible, varied teaching and assessment so all students have as equal a chance as possible, design for inclusion so alternative assessment is rarely needed and plan for the emotional impact of distressing material.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: monitoring assessment outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Assessment drives learning, progress and development, and serves to monitor progress, motivate, give feed-forward and grade against criteria; reasonable adjustments may be needed for inclusion, and course teams should monitor student outcomes, for example by protected characteristics, and reflect on assessment strategies.

forPractitioner.text: Monitor student outcomes, including by protected characteristics, to find unintended differences, reflect on assessment strategies and make reasonable adjustments to assessment where needed.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: scaffolded modules
statements.paraphrase: Modules in a criminology course should be scaffolded so that students can build on earlier learning as they progress.

forPractitioner.text: Scaffold modules so each builds on what students learned before, year on year.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: curricula enabling the honours outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Students are assessed against their curricula, which should let them reach the required outcomes and show the higher learning of an honours degree; at base every class shows the student has reached level 6 (England, Wales and Northern Ireland) or level 10 (Scotland).

forPractitioner.text: Design curricula so that students can reach the required outcomes and show honours-level learning; every class of degree, a third included, means level 6 (FHEQ) or level 10 (FQHEIS) has been met.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, set teaching and assessment so that every honours graduate can set out and look closely at the main concepts and theories of criminology, and judge how well they work when applied; this is the minimum for the award.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to set out and look closely at the main concepts and theories of criminology, and judge how well they work when applied.

statements.about: explaining and critically evaluating complex social problems
statements.paraphrase: At the typical (2:2 and 2:1) level, a graduate should be able to explain and judge critically complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level (2:2 and 2:1), most graduates should be able to explain and judge critically complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance; design assessment so they can show it.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the typical standard, you should be able to explain and judge critically complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the excellent level
statements.about: exceptional critical explanation of complex social problems
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent (first-class) level, a graduate should be able to explain and judge critically, to an exceptional standard, complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level (first class), graduates should be able to explain and judge critically, to an exceptional standard, complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance; design assessment with room to show it.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the excellent standard, you should be able to explain and judge critically, to an exceptional standard, complex social problems using criminological theories about crime, social class, victimisation and how societies respond to crime and deviance.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the threshold level
statements.about: analysing how criminology differs from other understandings
statements.paraphrase: At the threshold (third-class) level, a graduate should be able to analyse how criminology differs from other ways of understanding crime and society.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, set teaching and assessment so that every honours graduate can analyse how criminology differs from other ways of understanding crime and society; this is the minimum for the award.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to analyse how criminology differs from other ways of understanding crime and society.

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates at the typical level
statements.about: critically analysing how criminology differs from other understandings

statements.about: exceptional critical analysis of what sets criminology apart
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent (first-class) level, a graduate should be able to show an exceptionally critical analysis of how criminology differs from other ways of understanding crime and society.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level (first class), graduates should be able to show an exceptionally critical analysis of how criminology differs from other ways of understanding crime and society; design assessment with room to show it.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: systematic understanding of criminological topics
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to show systematic understanding of, and critical awareness about, topics shaped by criminology.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can show systematic understanding of, and critical awareness about, topics shaped by criminology; this adds to the honours outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course in criminology, you should be able to show systematic understanding of, and critical awareness about, topics shaped by criminology.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: history of ideas and social and political theory
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to show critical awareness of how ideas developed over time, their cultural setting and the social and political theories that shape criminological practice.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can show critical awareness of how ideas developed over time, their cultural setting and the social and political theories that shape criminological practice; this adds to the honours outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course in criminology, you should be able to show critical awareness of how ideas developed over time, their cultural setting and the social and political theories that shape criminological practice.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: the intersectionality of power
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to show critical awareness of how intersecting forms of power bear on criminal justice agencies and on responses to crime, harm, deviance and victimisation.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can show critical awareness of how intersecting forms of power bear on criminal justice agencies and on responses to crime, harm, deviance and victimisation; this adds to the honours outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course in criminology, you should be able to show critical awareness of how intersecting forms of power bear on criminal justice agencies and on responses to crime, harm, deviance and victimisation.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: methodologies and an own research design
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to pick suitable methodologies for complex problems and design an original research project.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can pick suitable methodologies for complex problems and design an original research project; this adds to the honours outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course in criminology, you should be able to pick suitable methodologies for complex problems and design an original research project.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: critical discussion, independence and originality
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to carry critical discussion and analysis of complex ideas forward and work independently with some originality.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can carry critical discussion and analysis of complex ideas forward and work independently with some originality; this adds to the honours outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course in criminology, you should be able to carry critical discussion and analysis of complex ideas forward and work independently with some originality.

statements.appliesTo: holders of a master's degree in criminology
statements.about: a substantial research project
statements.paraphrase: Beyond the honours outcomes, a master's graduate should be able to complete a substantial empirical project, systematic review or systematic case study grounded in broad current understanding of the subject.

forPractitioner.text: At master's level, make sure graduates can complete a substantial empirical project, systematic review or systematic case study grounded in broad current understanding of the subject; this adds to the honours outcomes.
